557	## First-time setup (config missing or invalid)
558	
559	If `live.mjs` outputs `{ ok: false, error: "config_missing" | "config_invalid", path }`, write the live config at the reported path. By default this is `.impeccable/live/config.json`.
560	
561	Schema:
562	
563	```json
564	{
565	  "files": ["<path-or-glob>", "<path-or-glob>", ...],
566	  "exclude": ["<optional-glob>", ...],
567	  "insertBefore": "</body>",
568	  "commentSyntax": "html",
569	  "cspChecked": true
570	}
571	```
572	
573	`files` is the inject target; **the HTML files the browser actually loads**, not necessarily source. Each entry is either a literal path (`"public/index.html"`) or a glob pattern (`"public/**/*.html"`). Tracked or generated doesn't matter here; wrap has its own generated-file guard and routes accepts through the fallback flow.
574	
575	`exclude` (optional) is a list of glob patterns matching files to skip, even if a `files` glob would have included them. Use for email templates, demo fixtures, or any HTML that isn't a live page.
576	
577	`cspChecked` tracks whether the CSP detection step below has already run. Absent on first setup; set to `true` after CSP is checked (whether patched, declined, or not needed).
578	
579	**Hard-excluded paths (cannot be overridden).** `**/node_modules/**` and `**/.git/**` are never matched regardless of what the user writes. These are vendor/metadata directories and injecting into them would silently instrument third-party code.
580	
581	**Glob syntax.** `**` matches any number of path segments (including zero), `*` matches any characters except `/`, `?` matches a single character except `/`. Paths are always relative to the project root with forward slashes.
582	
583	| Framework | `files` | `insertBefore` | `commentSyntax` |
584	|-----------|---------|----------------|-----------------|
585	| SPA with single shell (Vite / React / Plain HTML) | `["index.html"]` | `</body>` | `html` |
586	| Next.js (App Router) | `["app/layout.tsx"]` | `</body>` | `jsx` |
587	| Next.js (Pages) | `["pages/_document.tsx"]` | `</body>` | `jsx` |
588	| Nuxt | `["app.vue"]` | `</body>` | `html` |
589	| Svelte / SvelteKit | `["src/app.html"]` | `</body>` | `html` |
590	| Astro | `[" <root layout .astro>"]` | `</body>` | `html` |
591	| Multi-page (separate HTML per route) | `["public/**/*.html"]`: a glob covering the served directory | `</body>` | `html` |
592	
593	Pick an anchor that exists in every file (`</body>` almost always works). Use `insertAfter` if the anchor should match **after** a specific line.
594	
595	For multi-page sites, **prefer a glob over a literal file list**. New pages added later are picked up automatically on the next `live-inject.mjs` run; no config maintenance needed.
596	
597	For multi-page sites whose pages are *rebuilt* by a generator (Astro, static-site generators, custom scripts like `build-sub-pages.js`), the inject survives only until the next regeneration. Re-run `live.mjs` after each build. Accept is unaffected; it writes to true source via the fallback flow.

The spec does NOT have a Layout section. 101 102 ### Step 2b: Stage the frontmatter 103 104 From the auto-extracted tokens, draft the YAML frontmatter now (you'll write it at the top of DESIGN.md in Step 4). This is the machine-readable layer: what the live panel and Stitch's linter consume. 105 106 - **Colors**: one entry per extracted color. Key = descriptive slug (`oxblood-deep`, `editorial-magenta`, not `blue-800`). Value = whichever format the project treats as canonical (OKLCH or hex; see the frontmatter rules above). Don't split the source of truth: one format in the frontmatter, don't redefine the same token in prose with a different value. 107 - **Typography**: one entry per role (`display`, `headline`, `title`, `body`, `label`). Typography is an object; include only the props that are real for the project (`fontFamily`, `fontSize`, `fontWeight`, `lineHeight`, `letterSpacing`, `fontFeature`, `fontVariation`). 108 - **Rounded / Spacing**: whatever scale steps the project actually uses, keyed by whatever scale name the project uses (`sm` / `md` / `lg`, or `surface-sm`, or numeric steps). 109 - **Components**: one entry per variant (`button-primary`, `button-primary-hover`, `button-ghost`). transform: translateY(-2px); }" 279 } 280 ], 281 "narrative": { 282 "northStar": "The Editorial Sanctuary", 283 "overview": "2-3 paragraphs of the philosophy, pulled from DESIGN.md Overview section.", 284 "keyCharacteristics": ["...", "..."], 285 "rules": [{ "name": "The One Voice Rule", "body": "...", "section": "colors|typography|elevation" }], 286 "dos": ["Do use ..."], 287 "donts": ["Don't use ..."] 288 } 289 } 290 ``` 291 292 **What changed from schemaVersion 1.** The old sidecar carried token primitive arrays (`tokens.colors[]`, `tokens.typography[]`, etc.). Those values now live in the frontmatter. The sidecar only carries metadata that can't live in the frontmatter (tonal ramps, canonical OKLCH when the hex is an approximation, display names, role hints), keyed by the frontmatter token name (`colorMeta.`, `typographyMeta.`). Components still carry full HTML/CSS because Stitch's 8-prop set can't hold them. 293 294 #### Component translation rules 295 296 The `html` and `css` fields must be **self-contained, drop-in snippets** that render correctly when injected into a shadow DOM. The panel applies them directly: no post-processing, no framework runtime. 297 298 1. **Tailwind expansion.** If the source uses Tailwind (className="bg-primary text-white rounded-lg px-6 py-3"), expand every utility to literal CSS properties in the `css` string. Do **not** reference Tailwind classes; do **not** assume a Tailwind CSS bundle is loaded. Each component is self-contained. 299 2. **Token resolution.** If the project exposes tokens as CSS custom properties on `:root` (e.g. `--color-primary`, `--radius-md`), reference them via `var(--color-primary)`; they inherit through the shadow DOM and stay live-bound. If tokens live only in JS theme objects (styled-components, CSS-in-JS), resolve to literal values at generation time. 300 3. **Icons.** Inline as SVG. Do not reference Lucide/Heroicons packages, icon fonts, or ``. A typical icon is 16-24px; copy the SVG path data directly. 301 4. **States.** Include `:hover`, `:focus-visible`, and (if meaningful) `:active` rules inline. A static default-only snapshot makes the panel feel dead. Hover + focus rules in the CSS make it feel alive. 302 5. **Reset bloat.** Extract only the component's *distinctive* CSS (background, color, padding, border-radius, typography, transition). Skip universal resets (`box-sizing: border-box`, `line-height: inherit`, `-webkit-font-smoothing`). The panel already has a neutral canvas; don't re-ship resets. 303 6. **Scoped class names.** Prefix every class with `ds-` (e.g. `ds-btn-primary`, `ds-input-search`) so component CSS doesn't collide with other components' CSS in the same shadow DOM. 304 305 #### What to include 306 307 Aim for a tight set of **5-10 components** that best represent the visual system: 308 309 - **Canonical primitives (always include if the project has them):** button (each variant as a separate component entry), input/text field, navigation, chip/tag, card. 310 - **Signature components (include if distinctive):** hero CTA, featured card, filter pill, any custom pattern the user mentioned as important in PRODUCT.md. 311 - **Skip the rest.** Utility components, form building blocks, wrapper layouts: not worth documenting unless visually distinctive. 312 313 If the project has **no component library yet** (bare landing page, new project), synthesize canonical primitives from the tokens using best-practice defaults consistent with the DESIGN.md's rules. Every `.impeccable/design.json` has *something* to render, even on day zero. 314 315 #### Tonal ramps 316 317 For each color token, generate an 8-step `tonalRamp` array: dark to light, same hue and chroma, stepped lightness from ~15% to ~95%. The panel renders this as a strip under the swatch. If the project already defines a tonal scale (Material `surface-container-low` family, Tailwind-style `blue-50..blue-900`), use those values. Otherwise synthesize in OKLCH. 318 319 #### Narrative mapping 320 321 Pull directly from the DESIGN.md you just wrote: 322 323 - `narrative.northStar` → the `**Creative North Star: "..."**` line from Overview 324 - `narrative.overview` → the philosophy paragraphs from Overview 325 - `narrative.keyCharacteristics` → the bulleted `**Key Characteristics:**` list 326 - `narrative.rules` → every `**The [Name] Rule.** [body]` across all sections, tagged with `section` 327 - `narrative.dos` / `narrative.donts` → the bullet lists from Do's and Don'ts verbatim 328 329 Do not reword. The panel shows these as secondary collapsible context; the same voice that's in the Markdown carries through. 330 331 ### Step 5: Confirm and refine 332 333 1. Show the user the full DESIGN.md you wrote. Briefly highlight the non-obvious creative choices (descriptive color names, atmosphere language, named rules). 334 2. Mention that `.impeccable/design.json` was also written alongside; the live panel will now render this project's actual button/input/nav primitives instead of generic approximations. 335 3. Offer to refine any section: "Want me to revise a section, add component patterns I missed, or adjust the atmosphere language?" 336 337 Your own write is the freshest source; subsequent commands in this session don't need a reload. 338 339 ## Seed mode 340 341 For projects with no visual system to extract yet. Produces a minimal scaffold, not a full spec. 342 343 ### Step 1: Confirm seed mode 344 345 Before interviewing: "There's no existing visual system to scan. I'll ask five quick questions to seed a starter DESIGN.md. You can re-run `/impeccable document` once there's code, to capture the real tokens and components. OK?" 346 347 If the user prefers to skip, stop. No file. 348 349 ### Step 2: Five questions 350 351 Group into one `AskUserQuestion` interaction. Options must be concrete. 352 353 1. **Color strategy.** Pick one: 354 - Restrained: tinted neutrals + one accent ≤10% 355 - Committed: one saturated color carries 30–60% of the surface 356 - Full palette: 3–4 named color roles, each deliberate 357 - Drenched: the surface IS the color 358 359 Then: one hue family or anchor reference ("deep teal", "mustard", "Klim #ff4500 orange"). 360 361 2. **Typography direction.** Pick one (specific fonts come later): 362 - Serif display + sans body 363 - Single sans (warm / technical / geometric / humanist; pick a feel) 364 - Display + mono 365 - Mono-forward 366 - Editorial script + sans 367 368 3. **Motion energy.** Pick one: 369 - Restrained: state changes only 370 - Responsive: feedback + transitions, no choreography 371 - Choreographed: orchestrated entrances, scroll-driven sequences 372 373 4. **Three named references.** Brands, products, printed objects. Not adjectives. 374 375 5. **One anti-reference.** What it should NOT feel like. Also named. 376 377 ### Step 3: Write seed DESIGN.md 378 379 Use the six-section spec from Scan mode. Populate what the interview answers; leave the rest as honest placeholders. The seed is a scaffold, not a fabricated spec. 380 381 Lead the file with: 382 383 ```markdown 384 385 ``` 386 387 Per-section guidance in seed mode: 388 389 - **Overview**: Creative North Star and philosophy phrased from the answers (color strategy + motion energy + references). Reference the user's anti-reference directly. 390 - **Colors**: Color strategy as a Named Rule (e.g. *"The Drenched Rule. The surface IS the color."*). Hue family or anchor reference. No hex values; mark as `[to be resolved during implementation]`. 391 - **Typography**: the direction the user picked (e.g. "Serif display + sans body"). No font names yet: `[font pairing to be chosen at implementation]`. 392 - **Elevation**: inferred from motion energy. Restrained/Responsive → flat by default; Choreographed → layered. One sentence. 393 - **Components**: omit entirely; no components exist yet. 394 - **Do's and Don'ts**: carry PRODUCT.md's anti-references directly plus the anti-reference named in Q5. 395 396 Seed mode writes a minimal frontmatter with `name` and `description` only; no colors, typography, rounded, spacing, or components yet. Real tokens land on the next Scan-mode run. Skip the `.impeccable/design.json` sidecar in seed mode for the same reason: nothing to render. 397 398 ### Step 4: Confirm 399 400 1. Show the seed DESIGN.md. Call out that it is a seed (the marker is the literal commitment). 401 2. Tell the user: "Re-run `/impeccable document` once you have some code. That pass will extract real tokens and generate the sidecar." 402 403 Your own write is the freshest source; no reload needed. 404 405 ## Style guidelines 406 407 - **Frontmatter first, prose second.** Tokens go in the YAML frontmatter; prose contextualizes them. Don't redefine a token value in two places; the frontmatter is normative. 408 - **Cite PRODUCT.md anti-references by name** in the Do's and Don'ts section. If PRODUCT.md lists "SaaS landing-page clichés" or "generic AI tool marketing" as anti-references, the DESIGN.md Don'ts should repeat those phrases verbatim so the visual spec enforces the strategic line. 409 - **Match the spec, don't invent new sections.** The six section names are fixed. If you have Layout/Motion/Responsive content to document, fold it into Overview (philosophy-level rules) or Components (per-component behavior). 410 - **Descriptive > technical**: "Gently curved edges (8px radius)" > "rounded-lg". Include the technical value in parens, lead with the description. 411 - **Functional > decorative**: for each token, explain WHERE and WHY it's used, not just WHAT it is. 412 - **Exact values in parens**: hex codes, px/rem values, font weights; always the number in parens alongside the description. 413 - **Use Named Rules**: `**The [Name] Rule.** [short doctrine]`. These are memorable, citable, and much stickier for AI consumers than bullet lists. Stitch's own outputs use them heavily ("The No-Line Rule", "The Ghost Border Fallback"). Aim for 1-3 per section. 414 - **Be forceful**. The voice of a design director. "Prohibited", "forbidden", "never", "always", not "consider", "might", "prefer". Match PRODUCT.md's tone. 415 - **Concrete anti-pattern tests**. Stitch writes things like *"If it looks like a 2014 app, the shadow is too dark and the blur is too small."* A one-sentence audit test beats a paragraph of principle. 416 - **Reference PRODUCT.md**. The anti-references section of PRODUCT.md should directly inform the Do's and Don'ts section here. Quote or paraphrase. 417 - **Group colors by role**, not by hex-order or hue-order. Primary / Secondary / Tertiary / Neutral is the spec ordering. 418 419 ## Pitfalls 420 421 - Don't paste raw CSS class names. Translate to descriptive language. 422 - Don't extract every token. Stop at what's actually reused; one-offs pollute the system. 423 - Don't invent components that don't exist. If the project only has buttons and cards, only document those. 424 - Don't overwrite an existing DESIGN.md without asking. 425 - Don't duplicate content from PRODUCT.md. DESIGN.md is strictly visual. 426 - Don't add a "Layout Principles" or "Motion" or "Responsive Behavior" top-level section. The spec has six, not nine. Fold that content where it belongs. 427 - Don't rename sections even slightly. "Colors" not "Color Palette & Roles". "Typography" not "Typography Rules". Tooling parsing depends on exact headers. 428 - Don't duplicate token values between frontmatter and prose. If a color is in `colors.primary` as hex, the prose can name it and describe its role but should not reassert a different hex. The frontmatter is normative. 429 - Don't invent frontmatter token groups outside Stitch's schema (no `motion:`, `breakpoints:`, `shadows:` at the top level). Stitch's Zod schema only accepts `colors`, `typography`, `rounded`, `spacing`, `components`. Anything else belongs in the sidecar's `extensions`. 430

22	## CI/CD
23	CI runs on **tangled spindles** (`.tangled/workflows/`), not GitHub Actions. Three workflows, each running `just ci-relay` first (the Linux gate — like `just ci` but `--exclude identity-wallet`, since the iOS app needs the Apple/GTK toolchain absent in CI):
24	- `pr.yaml` — test gate on PRs to `main` (no deploy, no Railway token)
25	- `staging.yaml` — push to `main` → deploy to the Railway **staging** environment
26	- `release.yaml` — push a `v*` tag → promote to **production**

28	Deploys use the Railway CLI (nixpkgs dep) with environment-scoped tokens held as tangled repo secrets; production is reached only via a `v*` tag, never by merging to `main`. Litestream backs up the production SQLite DB. See [docs/deploy.md](docs/deploy.md).

31	- Managed entirely by Nix flake + devenv; do not install tools globally
32	- direnv auto-activates via `.envrc` (`use flake . --impure --accept-flake-config`)
33	- **Always run `nix develop` from the workspace root**, not from a subdirectory — `CARGO_HOME` and `RUSTUP_HOME` resolve relative to devenv root

BRAND SEED · seed-148

Seed color (anchor for your primary brand color):
  oklch(0.650 0.146 60.0) — orange / honey (one read: "Klim-style editorial gold — late-afternoon paper light on a serif specimen sheet, considered and dry")

This is the brand's anchor — a single beautiful color. Compose the rest of
the palette around it using YOUR judgment, the brief (PRODUCT.md /
DESIGN.md / the user's prompt), and the color-strategy guidance already in
SKILL.md.

How to use:

1. Read the brief. Write one specific phrase describing the mood this
   product calls for. Be granular. Good: "1970s travel poster — sun-baked
   warmth, considered", "midnight jazz club — smoky brass, saxophone
   light", "Scandinavian winter morning — quiet light through frost". Bad:
   "modern and clean", "warm and inviting". The first lets you compose; the
   second is generic and will produce generic palettes.

2. The seed's hue (60°) anchors your primary brand color. You
   choose L and C to match the mood. The same hue can be deep-and-velvet,
   bright-and-confident, or pale-and-faded — pick the one the mood demands.
   Primary's hue should stay within ±10° of the seed.
  - one example strategy: Hold the seed's amber as primary on a pure white page so the gold reads as ink rather than atmosphere, and pair with a deep aubergine accent for typographic contrast.

3. Now compose the full palette in OKLCH (5 more roles):
     • bg       — the most important architectural choice.
                  CORE PRINCIPLE: the mood lives in the BRAND COLORS
                  (primary + accent) and typography, NOT in the surface.
                  Stripe is warm — its purple does that, bg is pure
                  white. Linear is cool — its blue does that, bg is
                  pure. Notion is warm — its accents do that, bg is
                  near-pure-white. Putting warmth in BOTH primary AND
                  bg is the AI cliché.

                  DEFAULT A — PURE white: exactly oklch(1.000 0.000 0).
                    Not 0.99, not chroma 0.002. Stripe / Notion / Apple
                    use literal #ffffff. Don't add hidden warmth.
                    Refs: Stripe, Notion, Linear (light), Apple.com,
                    Vercel docs, Figma marketing, Loom, Substack.

                  DEFAULT B — PURE black/near-black: L 0.04-0.12,
                    chroma exactly 0.000. No hue tint. Vercel is
                    roughly oklch(0.08 0 0). Pick L for mood; C is 0.
                    Refs: Vercel, A24, Acne, Apple dark, MUBI.

                  ALT 2 — TINTED: chroma 0.015-0.05.
                    Use ONLY when:
                    (a) the mood is EXPLICITLY environmental — the surface
                        IS part of the brand (1920s lacquered interior,
                        leather library, ceramic studio, hotel lobby), or
                    (b) the seed itself is desaturated (chroma < 0.10) and
                        needs a tinted surface to read as a brand.
                    NOT for "feels warm" / "modern + warm" / "moody". If
                    your mood says "warm" but doesn't name a specific
                    environment, use PURE white and let primary carry
                    the warmth.

                  HEURISTIC: if seed chroma > 0.10 AND mood is product-
                  focused (not environment-focused), it's almost always
                  PURE white. Target distribution across many palettes:
                  ~50% pure white, ~25% pure black, ~25% tinted.
     • surface  — bg pulled slightly toward ink (10-15% mix). Same hue
                  family as bg. Used for cards, panels, sections.
     • ink      — body text color. Must reach ≥7:1 contrast vs bg.
                  Can carry the brand hue at low chroma in light mode
                  (slight warmth or coolness toward the brand).
     • accent   — a SECOND brand color, distinct from primary in BOTH
                  hue AND lightness. Picked to complement the mood (not
                  default-complementary across the wheel). Used for
                  badges, status pills, links, accent rules.
     • muted    — secondary text. Ink pulled 40% toward bg, keeping ink's
                  hue. Must reach ≥3.5:1 contrast vs bg.

4. Pick a color STRATEGY (the four steps from SKILL.md):
     • Restrained: tinted neutrals + accent ≤10% — product default
     • Committed: one saturated color carries 30-60% — identity-driven
     • Full palette: 3-4 named roles each used deliberately — brand work
     • Drenched: the surface IS the color — campaign, hero, statement
   The brief picks the strategy. A startup dashboard ≠ a perfume brand.

Hard rules (already in SKILL.md, recapped because the seed step is where
they actually bite):

  - OKLCH only — never hex. Never #RRGGBB.
  - ink-vs-bg WCAG contrast ≥ 7 (body text must be readable)
  - primary chroma ≤ 0.23 (above this, primary glows perceptually and
    no text on it is readable — acid-bright is a UI failure)
  - if primary L > 0.78, primary chroma ≤ 0.18 (the fluorescent zone)
  - primary-vs-accent contrast ≥ 1.7 (they must be visually distinct,
    not two variants of the same hue at similar lightness)
  - accent must carry readable text on a filled badge/pill: EITHER
    saturated (chroma ≥ 0.10) OR clearly light (L ≥ 0.85) OR clearly
    dark (L ≤ 0.30). Never a muddy mid-tone (L 0.45-0.72 + chroma < 0.10)
    — taupe/mushroom/dusty-grey accents read as weak and can't hold text
    either way. Saturate it or push its lightness to a clear light/dark.
  - avoid the saturated AI attractor zones: claude-beige (warm-cream bg
    + dusty brown primary), forest-green-on-cream, AI-purple-on-white,
    navy-cream-with-orange-accent

TEXT-ON-COLOR FILLS — pick by perceptual contrast, not just WCAG. The
rule applies to ANY element where text sits on a saturated color fill:
primary buttons, accent buttons, badges, status pills, tag highlights,
filled callouts. Don't only think "primary button" — apply consistently.

For any saturated mid-luminance color (L between 0.42 and 0.78, chroma ≥
0.08), use WHITE text (or near-white from your bg), not dark text — even
if WCAG says dark technically passes. The Helmholtz-Kohlrausch effect
makes saturated colors appear brighter than their luminance suggests,
and dark text on a warm-or-cool-saturated fill reads as muddy.

Convention: Stripe orange CTAs, McDonald's red, every fintech orange
button, Vercel's filled badges, Linear's status pills — all use white
text on saturated bg fills.

Dark text is correct only on PALE fills (L > 0.85) or PURE-NEUTRAL fills
(chroma near 0). Everything else: white text.

Return your composed palette in CSS custom properties using OKLCH, then
build with it. The seed is the start, not the recipe.

# Design System: Identity Wallet

## 1. Overview

**Creative North Star: "The Sealed Credential"**

This is the wax seal, the embossed foil on a passport, the notary's stamp — authenticity made visible, and held by the person it belongs to. The wallet guards the keys to someone's entire decentralized identity, so it must *feel* as rigorous as the cryptography beneath it: a serious security instrument, not an app with a lock icon. Gravitas here comes from precision and restraint — exact alignment, deliberate type, a monospace that tells the literal truth of a key — never from chrome, darkness, or decoration. It lives in the humane, light tradition of **Proton** and **1Password**: trustworthy without being cold, principled without being grim. The user should sit down and think *"this is solid; I understand what it's doing; my identity is genuinely safe here."*

Gold is the load-bearing idea, and it is gold-as-**authenticity**, never gold-as-money. Sealing-wax gold and aubergine on archival white evoke an official credential — a stamped, sovereign document — and pointedly reject the shiny, metallic, neon register of crypto. The surface stays pure white so the brand lives in the seal and the type, not in a tinted "warm" wash. The system is calm at rest and unmistakable under alarm: when an attacker touches the identity, a 72-hour clock starts, and every pixel on that path exists to make the stakes and the single right action impossible to misread.

This system explicitly rejects: **crypto/web3 hype** (neon, coins, gradients-to-the-moon), the **enterprise dashboard** (dense admin panels, SaaS-cream, chart-soup), anything **playful or gamified** (mascots, confetti, reward badges, rainbow avatars), **generic stock-iOS** (system blue, SF-only, 12px pills with no identity), and **Ledger-style dark-technical heaviness** (dark-by-default, asset-vault gloom).

**Key Characteristics:**
- Sealing-wax gold + aubergine on pure white — authenticity, not currency.
- A serious instrument: precision over polish, restraint over decoration.
- Light and humane (Proton / 1Password lane), never dark-and-heavy.
- Monospace tells the literal truth; progressive disclosure hides it until asked.
- Status is *never* color alone — it is color + icon + label + position.
- WCAG 2.2 AAA is the target, because a high-assurance tool owes a high-assurance interface.

## 2. Colors: The Sealed-Credential Palette

A two-brand-color system — sealing-wax gold and aubergine — on pure-white archival paper, with a disciplined status ramp reserved entirely for security state.

### Primary
- **Sealing-Wax Gold** (`oklch(0.46 0.105 62)`): the seal. Primary actions, the brand mark, the "verified/sealed" moment. Deliberately deep and dry — a brass-and-wax gold that holds near-white text (~5.5:1), not a bright leaf-gold that would read decorative or crypto. Pressed state **Deep Wax** (`oklch(0.38 0.090 60)`).
- **Pale Seal** (`oklch(0.92 0.055 80)`): the pale gold ground for small "sealed / verified" marks where dark ink text sits on top. The only place gold goes light.

### Secondary
- **Aubergine** (`oklch(0.34 0.10 330)`): the second brand voice and the color of *depth on demand*. Links, and the affordances that reveal cryptographic machinery (the "advanced / details" disclosures — DIDs, rotation keys, audit logs). A quiet nod to Proton's purple without copying it. Pressed state (`oklch(0.28 0.09 330)`).

### Neutral
- **Archival Ink** (`oklch(0.23 0.012 60)`): body text and headings. ~13:1 on white — comfortably AAA. Carries a barely-there warmth toward the brand hue so it never reads as cold pure-black.
- **Faded Ink** (`oklch(0.42 0.012 60)`): secondary labels and metadata (~5.6:1). Real body copy uses Archival Ink, not this, to hold the 7:1 AAA line.
- **Pure White** (`oklch(1 0 0)`): the page. No hidden warmth — the brand carries warmth, the surface does not.
- **Sealed Parchment** (`oklch(0.975 0.004 75)`) / **Sunk Parchment** (`oklch(0.955 0.005 75)`): cards, panels, and inset regions — the second neutral layer, a hair warm.
- **Hairline** (`oklch(0.90 0.004 75)`): 1px borders and dividers. Depth is a hairline and a tonal step, never a drop shadow at rest.

### Status (security signal only)
Each state is a **tonal pair**: a pale surface ground plus a deep same-hue ink/icon tone. This is what makes the badges AAA-legible *and* lets them coexist with a gold brand without confusion.
- **Verified Green** — ink `oklch(0.40 0.10 150)` on `oklch(0.95 0.045 150)`: a key the device authorized; the identity is safe.
- **Caution Amber** — ink `oklch(0.42 0.10 60)` on `oklch(0.95 0.055 75)`: attention needed; deep enough to never be mistaken for the brand gold.
- **Alarm Red** — ink `oklch(0.44 0.16 25)` on `oklch(0.95 0.045 25)`; solid fill **Alarm Solid** (`oklch(0.52 0.20 25)`) with near-white text for the override CTA: an unauthorized change, clock running.
- **Closed/Expired** — ink `oklch(0.42 0.02 25)` on `oklch(0.95 0.004 25)`: deliberately **ashen and desaturated** so an elapsed recovery window reads as *closed and inert*, not *act now*. It must not look like Alarm Red.
- **Calm Slate** — ink `oklch(0.42 0.07 250)` on `oklch(0.95 0.030 250)`: neutral information.

### Named Rules
**The Seal-vs-Signal Rule.** Gold is *identity*; the green/amber/red/slate ramp is *status*. Status colors always carry an icon and a text label and appear only in status contexts. Gold never masquerades as a status, and a status color never carries the brand.

**The Authenticity-Not-Currency Rule.** Gold is always matte, dry, editorial — a wax seal. Never metallic gradients, never coin shapes, never glint. The moment gold looks like money, it has become a crypto anti-reference.

**The Pure-Surface Rule.** The page is pure white (`oklch(1 0 0)`). Warmth comes from the seal and the type. Tinting the background "to feel warm" is forbidden — it's the AI-cream cliché and it muddies AAA contrast.

## 3. Typography

**Display / Body Font:** IBM Plex Sans (with `system-ui` fallback)
**Data / Mono Font:** IBM Plex Mono (with `ui-monospace` fallback)

**Character:** One superfamily, commissioned to express "the relationship between humans and machines" — precise but warm, engineered but humane. That is this product's brief almost verbatim: a serious instrument in a humane lane, with a monospace ready for the literal truth of a DID or a key. One sans carries headings, body, buttons, and labels; the mono is reserved for cryptographic literals — the machinery that progressive disclosure reveals. The scale is a **fixed rem** modular scale (~1.2 ratio), never fluid `clamp()`: users view at a consistent DPI, and a heading that shrinks in a panel looks worse, not better.

### Hierarchy
- **Display** (600, 1.75rem, 1.15): the one big moment per screen — a screen title, the wordmark. Mobile-restrained; no shouting hero scales.
- **Headline** (600, 1.375rem, 1.2): section and screen headings.
- **Title** (600, 1.125rem, 1.3): card titles, group headers, the handle on an identity.
- **Body** (400, 1rem, 1.55): prose and explanations. Cap measure at 65–75ch. Uses Archival Ink for the AAA 7:1 line.
- **Label** (500, 0.8125rem, +0.01em): buttons, field labels, metadata. Sentence case by default.
- **Data** (IBM Plex Mono, 0.875rem, 1.5): DIDs, public keys, CIDs, audit-log values — anything literal and verifiable. Always wraps with `break-all`; never truncates a key silently.

### Named Rules
**The Literal-Truth Rule.** Every cryptographic value — DID, rotation key, CID, signature — is set in IBM Plex Mono. Monospace signals "this is exact, verify it character by character." Proportional type is for prose, never for keys.

**The No-Eyebrow Rule.** No tiny uppercase tracked kicker above every section. One screen, one clear headline. Labels are sentence case; ALL-CAPS is reserved for nothing decorative.

## 4. Elevation

Flat by default. Depth is built from **tonal layers** (white page → parchment surface → sunk parchment) and **hairline borders**, not from drop shadows. A resting card is a parchment rectangle with a 1px hairline — no shadow. This is what keeps the system from sliding into either the 2014-app look or the enterprise card-soup look, and it reads as precise and instrument-grade.

Shadows appear only when an element genuinely floats above the page and the user must understand it as *temporary and modal*: the recovery-override confirmation sheet, and toasts. Two tokens, both soft and neutral — never colored, never decorative.

### Shadow Vocabulary
- **Sheet** (`box-shadow: 0 -8px 32px oklch(0.23 0.012 60 / 0.14)`): the override/confirmation sheet rising from the bottom.
- **Toast** (`box-shadow: 0 4px 20px oklch(0.23 0.012 60 / 0.16)`): transient status notifications.

### Named Rules
**The Flat-At-Rest Rule.** Surfaces are flat with a hairline at rest. A shadow is a response to *floating* (modal, toast) — a state, not a decoration. If a card has a shadow just sitting there, the shadow is wrong.

## 5. Components

Every interactive component ships its full state set — default, hover, focus-visible, active, disabled, loading, error — and the vocabulary is identical across every screen. A button that means "primary" looks the same in onboarding and on the alert screen.

### Buttons
- **Shape:** precise, not pill — 8px radius (`{rounded.md}`). Pointedly tighter than the stock-iOS 12px so it reads considered, not default.
- **Primary:** Sealing-Wax Gold fill, near-white label, 12px/20px padding. The seal. Hover → Deep Wax; active → Deep Wax + 1px inset; disabled → 40% toward parchment with Faded Ink label.
- **Secondary / Ghost:** Parchment fill, Archival Ink label, 1px hairline border. The quiet default for non-committing actions.
- **Destructive (Override):** Alarm-Solid fill, near-white label — used *only* for the irreversible recovery-override action, and only when the user has reviewed the operation. Gravity by scarcity.
- **Focus-visible:** a 2px Aubergine ring with a 2px offset on every interactive element — never removed. Visible keyboard focus is a security feature here, not a nicety.

### Cards / Containers
- **Corner Style:** 12px (`{rounded.lg}`).
- **Background:** Sealed Parchment on the white page.
- **Shadow Strategy:** none at rest (see Elevation).
- **Border:** 1px Hairline.
- **Internal Padding:** 20px (`lg`/`md`). Generous — depth comes from breathing room, not density. (Density is the enterprise anti-reference.)

### Inputs / Fields
- **Style:** white field, 1px Hairline, 8px radius, Archival Ink text.
- **Focus:** border shifts to Aubergine + the 2px focus ring. No glow.
- **Error:** Alarm-Red 1px border + a mono-or-sans error message in Alarm-Red ink, with an icon. Never color alone.
- **Mono fields:** inputs that accept a DID or handle use IBM Plex Mono.

### Status / Urgency Badge — *the signature component*
The crown jewel and the highest-stakes UI in the app. A badge that says how safe an identity is and, under attack, how long until the recovery window closes. **It is never color alone.** Each state is the union of four signals:

| State | Color (tonal pair) | Icon | Label | Position/behavior |
|-------|--------------------|------|-------|-------------------|
| Safe | Verified Green | ✓ shield | "Secure" | calm, static |
| Warning | Caution Amber | △ triangle | "Action needed" | — |
| Critical | Alarm Red | ◆ alert | live `"Xh Ym remaining"` | counts down every 60s |
| Expired | Ashen/Closed | ⊘ lock | "Recovery window closed" | inert, override disabled |

The countdown is announced to VoiceOver as text, not implied by a colored dot. Critical and Expired must be visually distinct — alarm vs. closed — so a colorblind user under attack can never confuse "act now" with "too late."

### DID Avatar
A deterministic identity mark — a hue derived by hash from the DID, so the same identity always renders the same color. Reconcile it with the system: constrain the derived color to the brand's chroma and a fixed lightness (e.g. `oklch(0.55 0.09 <hash-hue>)`), so a wall of identities reads as a coherent, muted set of seals — not rainbow confetti (which would be the playful anti-reference). The initial sits in IBM Plex Sans.

### Navigation
The app is a calm state-machine flow, not a chrome-heavy shell. A single back affordance (Aubergine, sentence-case "Back"), a clear screen title, and nothing competing with it. No tab bars of decorative icons, no persistent dense nav.

## 6. Do's and Don'ts

### Do:
- **Do** treat gold as a wax seal — matte, dry, editorial (`oklch(0.46 0.105 62)`). Authenticity, sovereignty, an official stamp.
- **Do** keep the page pure white (`oklch(1 0 0)`) and let the seal and type carry the brand.
- **Do** hold WCAG 2.2 AAA — Archival Ink body on white is ~13:1; verify every text-on-color pairing.
- **Do** signal status with color **and** an icon **and** a text label **and** position — always all four.
- **Do** keep Critical and Expired visually distinct: alarm-red that acts vs. ashen-slate that's closed.
- **Do** set every DID, key, CID, and signature in IBM Plex Mono — the literal truth, verifiable character by character.
- **Do** lead with plain human stakes ("someone is trying to take your identity") and tuck the cryptographic machinery one Aubergine tap behind a "details/advanced" disclosure.
- **Do** keep a visible 2px Aubergine focus ring on every interactive element.
- **Do** stay flat at rest; reserve the two soft shadows for floating sheets and toasts.

### Don't:
- **Don't** let gold look like money — no metallic gradients, coin shapes, glint, or "to the moon." The instant it reads as currency it has become the **crypto/web3** anti-reference.
- **Don't** build the **enterprise dashboard**: no dense admin panels, SaaS-cream backgrounds, or chart-soup. Reach depth by progressive disclosure, never by dumping density on screen one.
- **Don't** go **playful / gamified**: no mascots, confetti, reward badges, streaks, or rainbow avatars. Losing an identity to an attacker is too real to gamify.
- **Don't** ship **generic stock-iOS**: not system blue `#007aff`, not SF-only, not 12px pills on everything with no identity of its own.
- **Don't** go **Ledger-dark**: dark-technical, asset-vault heaviness is the wrong register. This is light and humane.
- **Don't** signal urgency by color alone — a colorblind user under attack must never have to guess.
- **Don't** tint the background "to feel warm" — that's the AI-cream cliché and it erodes contrast.
- **Don't** use a `border-left`/`border-right` colored stripe on cards or alerts; use a full 1px hairline, a tonal ground, or a leading icon.
- **Don't** use gradient-clipped text, decorative glassmorphism, or a big-number hero-metric template.
- **Don't** put a tiny uppercase tracked eyebrow above every section.

content.text:
Init is fully complete. Here's everything that's now in place, and the design decisions worth your eye.

## What got set up

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| [PRODUCT.md](PRODUCT.md) | Strategic source-of-truth: register, users, the 5 principles, anti-references, AAA. |
| [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) | The visual system — OKLCH tokens + the six Stitch-spec sections. |
| [.impeccable/design.json](.impeccable/design.json) | Sidecar: tonal ramps, motion/shadow tokens, drop-in component snippets, narrative. |
| [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) | Design Context pointer so any agent finds PRODUCT.md before touching the frontend. |
| [.impeccable/live/config.json](.impeccable/live/config.json) | Live mode pre-wired for the SvelteKit app. |

## The design choices I committed to (and why)

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
The whole system hangs on **reframing the one risky input into the strongest asset.** The palette seed was gold — which for a *security* product is a hair's breadth from the crypto-coin anti-reference. Rather than discard it, "The Sealed Credential" recasts gold as the wax seal / passport foil / notary stamp: the *original self-sovereign credential*. That single move turns the liability into the most on-brief idea in the system, and every other decision (matte not metallic, pure-white surface, aubergine for depth) falls out of protecting that frame.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

- **Status is now color-independent** — each state is color **+ icon + label + position**, fixing the AAA risk where the old code signalled urgency by color alone. And I split **critical** (alarm red, *act now*) from **expired** (ashen, *closed*) — the old code drew them identically, which could tell a panicking user the wrong thing.
- **Aubergine = the progressive-disclosure color** — it's reserved for the affordances that reveal the cryptographic machinery (DIDs, keys, audit logs), making "plain stakes first, depth one tap away" a visible rule.
- **IBM Plex Sans + Mono** — chosen because the superfamily was literally designed to express "humans and machines": precise but humane, with a mono ready for literal keys. It maps your brief almost verbatim.

## Two judgment calls to sanity-check

2. **IBM Plex's IBM association.** It earns its place, but if it brushes too close to your *enterprise* anti-reference, Hanken Grotesk or Geist (+ a mono) are clean swaps.

## 3. Typography

**Display / Body Font:** IBM Plex Sans (with `system-ui` fallback)
**Data / Mono Font:** IBM Plex Mono (with `ui-monospace` fallback)

The scale is a **fixed rem** modular scale (~1.2 ratio), never fluid `clamp()`: users view at a consistent DPI, and a heading that shrinks in a panel looks worse, not better.

### Hierarchy
- **Display** (600, 1.75rem, 1.15): the one big moment per screen — a screen title, the wordmark. Mobile-restrained; no shouting hero scales.
- **Headline** (600, 1.375rem, 1.2): section and screen headings.

## 3. Typography

**Display Font — the signet:** Libre Caslon Display, serif (with `Georgia` fallback)
**UI / Body Font:** Public Sans (with `system-ui` fallback)
**Data / Mono Font:** JetBrains Mono (with `ui-monospace` fallback)

**Character:** A three-font system that stages the metaphor. **Public Sans** — the typeface of the U.S. government design system, the sober workhorse of official identity documents — carries every working surface: headings, body, buttons, labels. It reads sovereign and trustworthy, with neither brand-y warmth nor enterprise chill. Above it, **Libre Caslon Display** is the *signet*: an engraved old-style serif (Caslon set the Declaration of Independence) reserved for the single ceremonial display moment on a screen — the wordmark, a hero line, an identity's monogram. Its rarity is what makes it read as a stamped seal rather than decoration. **JetBrains Mono** carries the literal truth — DIDs, keys, CIDs — with a tall x-height and unmistakable character shapes built for reading code under pressure. The scale is a **fixed rem** modular scale (~1.2 ratio), never fluid `clamp()`: users view at a consistent DPI, and a heading that shrinks in a panel looks worse, not better.

### Hierarchy
- **Display** (Libre Caslon Display, 400, 1.75rem, 1.15): the one signet moment per screen — the wordmark, a hero line, a document title. Serif. Mobile-restrained; no shouting hero scales.
- **Headline** (Public Sans, 600, 1.375rem, 1.2): section and screen headings — the working voice.
- **Title** (Public Sans, 600, 1.125rem, 1.3): card titles, group headers, the handle on an identity.
- **Body** (Public Sans, 400, 1rem, 1.55): prose and explanations. Cap measure at 65–75ch. Uses Archival Ink for the AAA 7:1 line.
- **Label** (Public Sans, 500, 0.8125rem, +0.01em): buttons, field labels, metadata. Sentence case by default.
- **Data** (JetBrains Mono, 0.875rem, 1.5): DIDs, public keys, CIDs, audit-log values — anything literal and verifiable. Always wraps with `break-all`; never truncates a key silently.

### Named Rules
**The Signet Rule.** Libre Caslon Display appears at most once per screen, for the single ceremonial display moment. Everything that works — headings, labels, buttons, data — is Public Sans or JetBrains Mono. The serif is a seal, and a seal you stamp twice is a smudge.

**The Literal-Truth Rule.** Every cryptographic value — DID, rotation key, CID, signature — is set in JetBrains Mono. Monospace signals "this is exact, verify it character by character." Proportional type is for prose, never for keys.

**The No-Eyebrow Rule.** No tiny uppercase tracked kicker above every section. One screen, one clear headline. Labels are sentence case; ALL-CAPS is reserved for nothing decorative.

content.text:
Here's the security-alert screen — [docs/design/security-alert-mock.html](docs/design/security-alert-mock.html). What it puts to the test, and what to look at:

**The decisions you can't see just by glancing:**
- **One signet, spent well.** Caslon appears exactly once — the headline *"Someone changed your identity."* Everything operational is Public Sans; the keys and CID are JetBrains Mono. The engraved serif on the gravest line reads as composure, not panic.
- **Threat is red; your defense is gold.** The countdown, status pill, and progress bar carry red (the attack). The primary action is the *gold seal* — "Review & override" — because reclaiming your identity is stamping it with your own signet, not a "destructive" act. Red is never spent on the button that saves you.
- **Status survives colorblindness.** "Recovery window closing" is red **+** the octagon icon **+** the words **+** the shrinking bar **+** the live `02:46:58`. Drop the color entirely and it still reads as critical.
- **Progressive disclosure is literal.** Plain language first ("a key your device doesn't recognize — so it wasn't you"); the DIDs, CID, and the `+ rotationKey` diff are one tap behind *View the technical change*.
- **The counterweight to panic** is the shield line: *"your posts, follows, and data are untouched."* Calm under alarm, in one sentence.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
Building this surfaced a real flaw in the *existing* model worth flagging: the current `deadline.ts` thresholds map ≥24h remaining to **`safe` (green)**. On the home screen that's fine, but on an *alert* screen it would paint a green "Secure" badge over an identity that's actively under attack — just because there's time left. Color is encoding *time-pressure* while the user reads it as *threat level*. The fix is a separate alert-screen vocabulary ("ample time / act soon / closing / closed") rather than reusing the home-screen safe→critical ramp. That's a DESIGN.md + `deadline.ts` refinement, not a blocker.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Where to go next — your call:
- **Refine this screen** — tune copy, the countdown treatment, density, anything that feels off.
- **Build the next step in the flow** — the **Review & override confirm** screen, where the irreversible red destructive button actually lives (the one this screen leads to).

# Working with Devenv

## Overview

**devenv** manages project dependencies through Nix. Commands like `pnpm`, `node`, `turbo` live in `.devenv/profile/bin/` and are only available inside a devenv shell.

**Core principle:** Verify you're in devenv before running managed commands. Never manually modify PATH.

## Quick Reference

| Task | Command | When |
|------|---------|------|
| Check if in devenv | `echo $DEVENV_STATE` | Shows path if active, empty if not |
| Enter interactive shell | `devenv shell` | For multiple commands, development work |
| Run single command | `devenv shell -c "command"` | One-off execution, CI scripts |
| Auto-activate (best) | `direnv allow` (once) | Automatic activation on `cd` |
| Exit devenv shell | `exit` | Leave interactive shell |

## Patterns

### Interactive Development

```bash
devenv shell      # Enter shell once
pnpm install      # Run multiple commands
pnpm build
pnpm test
exit              # Leave when done
```

### One-Off Commands

```bash
devenv shell -c "pnpm build"                        # Single command
devenv shell -c "pnpm install && pnpm build"        # Chain commands
```

### Scripts and Automation

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -e

# Auto-activate devenv if not already in it
if [ -z "$DEVENV_STATE" ]; then
  exec devenv shell -c " $@"
fi

# Rest of script runs with devenv active
pnpm install && pnpm build && pnpm test
```

**Why `exec`:** Replaces current process instead of nesting shells.

### Automatic Activation with direnv (Best Practice)

**Setup once:**
```bash
brew install direnv                           # Install direnv
echo 'eval "$(direnv hook zsh)"' >> ~/.zshrc  # Hook into shell (or bash)
source ~/.zshrc                               # Reload config
cd /path/to/project                           # Navigate to project
direnv allow                                  # Allow activation
```

**Then just use commands:**
```bash
cd /path/to/project   # Automatically activates devenv
pnpm build            # Commands work immediately
```

**Advantages:** No manual `devenv shell`, auto-activates/deactivates on `cd`, team consistency.

**Note:** If project has `.envrc` file, it's already configured for direnv.

## Common Mistakes

### ❌ Manual PATH Modification

```bash
# DON'T
export PATH=.devenv/profile/bin:$PATH
PATH=.devenv/profile/bin:$PATH pnpm build
```

**Why wrong:** `.devenv/profile/bin/` paths change on updates, bypasses environment setup, breaks if devenv not built.

**Do instead:** `devenv shell -c "pnpm build"` or use direnv.

### ❌ Global Package Installation

```bash
# DON'T
npm install -g turbo
pnpm add -g some-package
```

**Why wrong:** devenv manages dependencies via Nix. Global installs create version conflicts, not reproducible.

**Do instead:** Check if in devenv first, or add to `devenv.nix`.

### ❌ Nested Shells

```bash
# DON'T enter devenv when already in devenv
devenv shell  # Creates nested shell
```

**Why wrong:** Wastes resources, confusing exit behavior.

**Do instead:** Check `$DEVENV_STATE` first: `[ -n "$DEVENV_STATE" ] && echo "Already in devenv"`

### ❌ Assuming Commands Are Available

```bash
# DON'T run without checking environment
pnpm build  # Might work, might not
```

**Why wrong:** Inconsistent behavior, fails for others/CI.

**Do instead:** Use `devenv shell -c` or verify `$DEVENV_STATE` first.

## Troubleshooting

**Command not found after entering devenv:**
- Run `devenv update` to rebuild environment
- Verify `.devenv/` directory exists

**Nested shell confusion:**
- Check depth: `echo $SHLVL`
- Exit to fresh shell: `exec bash`

**PATH seems wrong:**
- Never modify PATH manually - let devenv manage it
- Rebuild: `devenv update`

## When NOT to Use

- Already in devenv (check `$DEVENV_STATE` first)
- System commands (`ls`, `grep`, `git` don't need devenv)
- Other project's commands (only use for current project)

its brand type **offline** — a Tauri WKWebView loads from disk with no web server,

The token layer is **real and verified**. Here's the milestone.

## What's now live in the app

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| [tokens.css](apps/identity-wallet/src/lib/styles/tokens.css) | The design system as code — OKLCH palette, type scale, spacing, radii, shadows, motion, semantic z-index. The single source of truth. |
| [fonts.css](apps/identity-wallet/src/lib/styles/fonts.css) | Self-hosted `@font-face` for all three families. |
| [base.css](apps/identity-wallet/src/lib/styles/base.css) | Reset, body defaults, the AAA aubergine focus ring, reduced-motion, `color-scheme: light`. |
| [static/fonts/](apps/identity-wallet/static/fonts/) | 7 real font files (~420KB), bundled offline. |
| [+layout.svelte](apps/identity-wallet/src/routes/+layout.svelte) | Imports the three layers globally. |
| [ModeSelectScreen](apps/identity-wallet/src/lib/components/onboarding/ModeSelectScreen.svelte) · [DIDAvatar](apps/identity-wallet/src/lib/components/home/DIDAvatar.svelte) | Converted to tokens — the adoption pattern + the entry screen and the seal monogram, now real. |

**Verification (not a claim — I ran it):** `pnpm build` passed — 260 modules transformed, written to `dist`. `--color-primary: oklch(.46 .105 62)` and the focus ring are in the bundled CSS; all 7 fonts copied to `dist/fonts/`. It builds and bundles offline. *(One note: I had to run the build with the sandbox off — Nix needs to write its cache at `~/.cache/nix/`, outside the sandbox's writable paths. Manage that anytime via `/sandbox`.)*

I also recorded the token layer as a contract in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) — "reference `var(--…)`, never hardcode hex/px" — so future work extends the system instead of re-fragmenting it.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
CSS custom properties are the right substrate for this bridge specifically because they're **late-bound and inheritable**: a component's scoped `<style>` can reference `var(--color-critical)` and stay fully encapsulated, yet every such reference resolves to one definition. That's how 25 components migrate *incrementally* — each one swaps its hexes for tokens on its own schedule, with zero coordination — and the moment they do, the alert-red that fractured across screens in the original crawl can only ever have one value again. The DESIGN.md was the law; this file is the enforcement.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

This is a genuine milestone: the system is no longer just docs and mocks — it's **running code, verified**. The remaining ~23 components still carry their old hexes; migrating them (ideally bringing the four mocked screens into real Svelte, since those designs are already worked out) is the natural continuation, and it's now mechanical rather than creative.

Want to keep going — port the **identity-list home** or the **alert/recovery flow** into real components next — or is this a good place to pause? Either way, you've taken this from a blank `init` to a coherent, shipping-ready design foundation.
Yes, please keep going!

Let me port a mocked screen into the real app. I'll start with the **identity-list home** — it's the foundational, most-seen screen, and it already uses the `DIDAvatar` I converted. The critical difference from the mock: this is a *real* component with actual prop contracts, data bindings, and navigation callbacks I must preserve exactly while applying the design. Let me read it and how it's wired.

This is the real thing — the actual `IdentityListHome`, with live IPC data, alert-event listeners, and navigation callbacks. The key reconciliation: my mock simplified status to "Secure," but the real component carries **two distinct status dimensions** — rotation-key custody (`Root key` / `Not root` / `Unknown`) *and* security alerts (clickable, → `onalert`). I'll preserve all of that logic and apply the design, deriving the calm "all secure" affirmation from real alert state.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
This is where porting a mock differs fundamentally from making one: the mock owns its data, but a real component's data shape is *non-negotiable* — `deviceKeyIsRoot: boolean | null`, an `alertData` Map fed by a `plc_alert` Tauri event listener, three loading states. The design has to bend to the data, not the reverse. So the "all identities secure" banner can't be decorative — it has to be `$derived` from whether `alertData` is empty, or it would lie. Honest-never-hype, enforced in code.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

I'll keep the entire data-loading script intact, add a small derived alert count + a host-extraction helper, and rewrite the markup and styles onto the tokens.

content.text:
## Identity-list home — ported to the real app

[IdentityListHome.svelte](apps/identity-wallet/src/lib/components/home/IdentityListHome.svelte) now renders the approved design on live data. What the port had to reconcile beyond the mock:

- **Two real status dimensions, both preserved:** the rotation-key custody badge (`Root key` green / `Not root` amber / `Unknown` neutral) *and* the clickable alert badge (critical) that still fires `onalert`. Each is color **+ icon + label** — colorblind-safe.
- **The monitoring banner is `$derived`, not decorative:** "All identities secure / Watching the public record" only when `alertData` is genuinely empty; otherwise it flips to a critical "N unauthorized changes need your attention." It can't lie.
- **All three states got the design:** a tokenized skeleton for loading (product-register-correct, not a spinner), and on-brand empty + error states.
- **Zero logic touched:** `listIdentities`, the `plc_alert` event listener, `onselect`/`onadd`/`onalert`, the degraded-card fallback — all intact. Only the seal `DIDAvatar` (already converted) and the markup/styles changed.

**Verified:** `pnpm check` (types, clean) + `pnpm build` both pass.

One honesty note on verification: I can't render this one in the Launch preview the way I did the mocks. The home calls Tauri IPC (`listIdentities`, `checkIdentityStatus`) that only exists inside the app, so it shows live only via the iOS simulator (`just ios-dev`) — a plain browser would hang on the IPC. So the proof here is the passing type-check + build plus fidelity to the mock you already approved, not a fresh screenshot.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
This is the moment the token layer proves its worth under real conditions. The home's old code hardcoded `#007aff`, `#dcfce7`, `#f59e0b`, `#991b1b` — the exact fragmented palette the first crawl flagged. Now every one of those is a `var(--color-*)` resolving to the single source of truth, so the green here and the green on the alert screen are *provably* the same green. The migration cost was one file; the consistency guarantee is permanent.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Next in line is the **alert/recovery flow** — `AlertDetailScreen` + `RecoveryOverrideScreen`, the two real components behind the dramatic mocks (including porting that hold-to-confirm into real code). Want me to take those on next, or pause here to eyeball the home in the simulator first?
Simulator is looking great! I had to create an account which took me mostly through the onboarding flows which we haven't updated yet. everything else though, chef's kiss!

Ha — chef's kiss, I'll take it. And that's exactly the right catch: account creation runs through the ~12 onboarding screens, which are still on the old hardcoded hexes — so the moment you leave `ModeSelect` and the home, you fall back into generic-iOS land. That inconsistency is now the most visible gap, and it's the first thing every *new* user sees. Let's fix the whole create flow.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
The smart way to migrate ~12 onboarding screens isn't twelve one-off restyles — it's to notice they're almost all the same skeleton (back · title · subtitle · input(s) · primary action · error) and **extract that skeleton into shared primitives** first: an `OnboardingShell`, a `TextField`, a `Button`. Then each screen migration becomes "wrap in Shell, swap inputs for TextField" — fast *and* consistent by construction. That simultaneously kills the duplication the very first crawl flagged (the blue button redefined N times) — one migration, two wins.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Let me read a representative spread of the create-flow screens to design primitives that fit all of them.

The pattern is crystal-clear and remarkably uniform: a centered screen, a title, a muted hint, optional input(s) with `#ef4444` error states, and a `#007aff` primary button with a `#9ca3af` disabled state — repeated verbatim across every screen. That's textbook duplication begging for extraction. The primitives write themselves: `OnboardingShell`, `TextField`, `Button`, plus a `SealEmblem` (the gold wax mark already recurring in ModeSelect/success/ceremony). Let me read the remaining pure-form screens so I migrate them in the same pass.

All nine confirm the same skeleton (with two genuinely-special inputs: the relay URL and the 6-char claim code). That's enough to design five primitives that cover everything. Let me build the shared UI layer, then migrate the create-flow screens onto it.

<script lang="ts">
  import { saveRelayUrl, type RelayConfigError } from '$lib/ipc';
  import OnboardingShell from '$lib/components/ui/OnboardingShell.svelte';
  import TextField from '$lib/components/ui/TextField.svelte';
  import Button from '$lib/components/ui/Button.svelte';
  import Spinner from '$lib/components/ui/Spinner.svelte';

  const DEFAULT_RELAY_URL = 'https://relay.ezpds.com';

  let { onnext }: { onnext: () => void } = $props();

  let url = $state(DEFAULT_RELAY_URL);
  let loading = $state(false);
  let error = $state<string | undefined>(undefined);

  let isValidFormat = $derived(
    url.trim().length > 0 &&
      (url.startsWith('http://') || url.startsWith('https://'))
  );

  async function handleConnect() {
    error = undefined;
    loading = true;
    try {
      await saveRelayUrl(url.trim());
      onnext();
    } catch (e) {
      const relayError = e as RelayConfigError;
      if (relayError.code === 'INVALID_URL') {
        error = 'Invalid URL — must start with http:// or https://';
      } else if (relayError.code === 'KEYCHAIN_ERROR') {
        error = 'Could not save the relay URL. Please try again.';
      } else {
        error = 'Could not reach the relay. Check the URL and try again.';
      }
    } finally {
      loading = false;
    }
  }
</script>

<OnboardingShell
  title="Connect to a relay"
  subtitle="Your wallet connects to a relay to create your identity. Use the default, or enter the address of your own."
>
  <TextField
    bind:value={url}
    type="url"
    mono
    disabled={loading}
    placeholder="https://relay.ezpds.com"
    autocomplete="off"
    autocorrect="off"
    autocapitalize="off"
    spellcheck={false}
    aria-label="Relay URL"
    {error}
  />
  {#if loading}
    <Spinner label="Connecting…" />
  {:else}
    <Button disabled={!isValidFormat} onclick={handleConnect}>Connect</Button>
  {/if}
</OnboardingShell>

## Create-onboarding flow — migrated

**5 shared primitives** now live in [src/lib/components/ui/](apps/identity-wallet/src/lib/components/ui/): `Button`, `TextField`, `Spinner`, `SealEmblem`, `OnboardingShell`. And **10 screens** rebuilt on them: ModeSelect, Welcome, RelayConfig, ClaimCode, Email, Handle, Password, Loading, Authenticating, DIDSuccess.

**Verified:** `svelte-check` → 0 errors, build → `dist` written. All prop contracts, validation logic, and IPC calls (`saveRelayUrl`, `startOAuthFlow`, clipboard) preserved exactly — only markup and styles changed.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
This is the extraction the very first codebase crawl predicted paying off. The `#007aff` primary button was hand-redefined in ~10 files; the muted hint, the `#ef4444` error text, the `2px #d1d5db` input — all duplicated verbatim per screen. Now there's **one** `Button`, **one** `TextField`, **one** error treatment. The migration didn't just retheme — it deleted the duplication that made the inconsistency *possible*. Change the button's pressed state once and all ten screens move together. That's the difference between a reskin and a system.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**What you'll see in the simulator now:** the create flow is consistent end-to-end *except* three screens I deliberately left for special treatment — `did_ceremony`, `shamir_backup`, and `handle_registration`. Now there's one `DiffRow` primitive (full tonal grounds, leading icons), and I retrofitted `RecoveryOverrideScreen` onto it too — so the operation-diff vocabulary is identical whether you're claiming an identity or reclaiming one from an attacker.
- **`TextField` grew an `oninput` hook** so `IdentityInput` can clear a stale resolution as you type — without abandoning the shared component.

**Verified:** `svelte-check` → **0 errors, 0 warnings across 331 files**, build clean.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
Step back and look at what the primitive layer became: **7 components** — `Button`, `TextField`, `Spinner`, `SealEmblem`, `OnboardingShell`, `UrgencyBadge`, `DiffRow` — now compose ~20 screens. The claim flow and the recovery flow, written months apart by the look of them, turned out to be the *same shapes*: a diff to review, a countdown to respect, a destructive confirm. The migration didn't just repaint them — it revealed they were one design problem wearing two costumes, and now they share the solution. # Done — the whole app is on the design system

That's the finish line. Every screen the app can render now speaks "The Sealed Credential," and there isn't a single hardcoded hex left in the component tree.

**The arc, start to finish:**

| Phase | What landed |
|---|---|
| **Strategy** | [PRODUCT.md](PRODUCT.md), [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) + [sidecar](.impeccable/design.json), font proposals, live-mode config |
| **Direction** | 4 interactive mocks (alert · override · home · ceremony) — validated the system before any real code |
| **Foundation** | Token layer ([tokens](apps/identity-wallet/src/lib/styles/tokens.css)/[fonts](apps/identity-wallet/src/lib/styles/fonts.css)/[base](apps/identity-wallet/src/lib/styles/base.css)) + 7 self-hosted woff2 fonts, bundled offline |
| **Primitives** | `Button`, `TextField`, `Spinner`, `SealEmblem`, `OnboardingShell`, `UrgencyBadge`, `DiffRow` |
| **Migration** | ~25 components: both onboarding paths (create + import), home, identity detail, the alert→override→reclaim spine, and the legacy/root screens |

**Highlights that became real code, not just mocks:**
- The **wax-seal hold-to-press** mints a DID (`performDIDCeremony`); the **red hold-to-override** submits the real `submitRecoveryOverride`. Same gesture, opposite emotional key.
- Two genuine bugs fixed along the way: the `createdAt` reactivity freeze, and a `string | null` endpoint leaking into the UI.
- "Green while under attack" corrected once, in `UrgencyBadge`, and it propagated everywhere.

**Evidence (all run, not asserted):** `svelte-check` → **0 errors, 0 warnings across 331 files**; `vite build` → clean, fonts bundled into `dist/`; hex grep → **empty**.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
The deepest proof this worked isn't the screenshots — it's that **the duplication that caused the original inconsistency is gone**. The first crawl found `#007aff` redefined in ~20 files and a fragmented green/amber/red. Now there's one `Button`, one `UrgencyBadge`, one `DiffRow`, one source of truth per token. The app didn't just get repainted; it got a spine. The next person who tweaks the brand gold edits one line and the whole app moves — which is the difference between a coat of paint and a design system.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**Where to go from here — your call:**
- **Test the full flows in the simulator** — both create *and* import end to end, plus the ceremony hold and an alert→override run, now that every screen is consistent.
- **Commit it.** This is a large, coherent change sitting on `main` — I'd suggest a branch + a structured commit (or a PR). I can stage that whenever you're ready, but I'll wait for your go since it's your call how to land it.
- **Polish pass** — if anything looks off in the simulator, point me at it and I'll tune. (A couple of candidates worth a look: a real dark-mode story someday, and whether the alert-screen `safe`→slate vocabulary reads right in practice.)

content.text:
Here's the relay OAuth flow on the design system — [docs/design/relay-oauth-mock.html](docs/design/relay-oauth-mock.html). Three states: sign-in/consent, the wrong-credentials state, and the unsafe-request error page.

**What changed from the neobrutalist original:**
- **Visual continuity with the wallet** — the same sealing-wax seal, Caslon headline, Public Sans body, and JetBrains Mono for the handle/DID and the client ID. Land here mid-OAuth and it's unmistakably the *same* product, which is the whole point: continuity is a trust signal at the password moment.
- **The consent *is* a seal.** Approve is the gold seal button with the shield mark — you're pressing your signet to authorize the app. Deny is a quiet ghost.
- **Clear "who's asking."** The app gets an aubergine monogram + name + client ID (mono), so it's obvious *which* app you're authorizing.
- **Honest permissions.** Raw scopes (`atproto`, `transition:generic`) as mono chips, plus a plain-language line translating what they actually grant.
- **Trust + safety cues.** A `relay.ezpds.com` footer with a lock so you can verify you're on the real relay; the error states are color-independent (icon + text), and the unsafe-request page explains *why* it stopped in plain words.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
Two things on this surface aren't pure aesthetics and deserve your call. **(1) Button weight:** I made Approve visually dominant (wider, gold). That's friendly for *your* wallet, but on a generic OAuth consent screen, nudging toward "approve" edges toward a dark pattern — equal-weight Deny/Approve is the more principled default. **(2) Font delivery:** the wallet bundles fonts offline, but this page renders in Safari from the relay. Using Google Fonts would leak every login to Google — wrong for a privacy-minded auth page — so the real implementation should self-host (a tiny `/oauth/fonts` route, or base64-embed at least Caslon and fall back to system-ui for the rest to keep page weight sane).
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

How does it land? And any preference on the two calls above — **Approve-emphasized vs. equal-weight buttons**, and **how self-hosted fonts should be served**?

That's the real blocker, and it's not the code: **the disk is full.** The `Data` volume is at **100%** with only ~**257 MiB free** across all volumes. SQLite's "database or disk is full" is literal — `nix develop` can't even write its fetcher cache to enter the shell, so `cargo` never ran. (The nix cache itself is only 582 MB — not the culprit; it's the 420 GiB used on your Data volume.)

I won't delete anything to claw back space — that's your call, and nothing I'd touch safely frees gigabytes. So here's where things stand, honestly:

**The implementation is written** (and `cargo fmt` *did* run and reformat it — which means it's at least syntactically valid Rust, since rustfmt won't parse a broken file). What I changed:

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| [static_assets.rs](crates/relay/src/routes/static_assets.rs) | New `GET /static/*path` — serves the brand fonts, embedded via `include_bytes!` (no asset dir needed in the container), long immutable cache, 404 for anything else. + 2 tests. |
| [app.rs](crates/relay/src/app.rs) | Registered the route + import. |
| [routes/mod.rs](crates/relay/src/routes/mod.rs) | Declared the module. |
| [oauth_templates.rs](crates/relay/src/routes/oauth_templates.rs) | Full Sealed-Credential redesign of the consent + error pages, **equal-weight** Deny/Approve, fonts from `/static/fonts`. Form contract (action, 7 hidden inputs, `identifier`/`password`, `approve`/`deny`) and `html_escape` on every user value preserved. |
| [crates/relay/assets/fonts/](crates/relay/assets/fonts/) | The 7 woff2/ttf files. |

**What I could *not* do: verify the build.** I'm not going to claim it compiles or passes tests — I genuinely couldn't run either. Once you free some disk space, the check is:

The approved mock (equal-weight buttons) is the design-of-record at [docs/design/relay-oauth-mock.html](docs/design/relay-oauth-mock.html).

The app *and* the login handoff now speak one language.
